lesson: In advance(), enforce the complete lifecycle transition map where paid orders can only move to shipped or on_hold, rejecting direct transitions from paid to cancelled.
why: A charged order must be placed on hold first so the charge can settle before cancellation.
quote: a charged order can NEVER move straight to cancelled; it has to be put on_hold first so the charge settles before anyone cancels.

lesson: When advance() blocks an invalid move, it must raise InvalidTransition and emit a warning log containing only the order id and attempted pair, omitting all payload fields.
why: Support relies on the log for triaging, but payload fields must be excluded because they contain sensitive customer data.
quote: Raise InvalidTransition and also log at warning with the order id and the attempted pair - support triages from that log. No payload fields

lesson: In advance(), refunded can strictly only be reached from returned; direct transitions from shipped to refunded are rejected, requiring carrier-lost parcels to be marked returned first.
why: Direct shipped-to-refunded shortcuts caused duplicate refunds when concurrent refund flows were triggered off shipments and returns.
quote: No direct shipped->refunded, ever - that shortcut is exactly how the double refund happened: one path refunding via the return flow

lesson: In advance(), on_hold orders must only transition to pending or cancelled (not back to paid), while cancelled and refunded are terminal states.
why: Orders were getting stuck on hold because prior logic viewed exiting on_hold as moving backwards.
quote: on_hold releases back to pending, or goes to cancelled. That's the stuck-order complaint, incidentally

lesson: advance() must refuse unknown or legacy states not present in the transition map by raising InvalidTransition instead of attempting in-place repairs.
why: advance() acts strictly as a state guard rather than a migration tool, and ancient row cleanup is managed separately by the data team.
quote: advance() is a guard, not a migration; the data team owns cleaning up ancient rows and there's a separate backfill for that.

lesson: In advance(), compare both the stored state and incoming target state case-insensitively, and always persist the target status in lowercase canonical form.
why: Legacy database rows contain mixed-case statuses, and persisting canonical lowercase values ensures the table converges over time.
quote: Compare BOTH sides case-insensitively: the current state and the target. And whatever advance() stores must be the lowercase canonical form
